proposals.before: Subordinate Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi fought over Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Liu at Shenshan Temple and, pressing his advantage, moved to attack Heyang, encamping at Luokou.
proposals.after: Subordinate Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi fought over Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Liu at Shengshan Temple and, pressing his advantage, moved to attack Heyang, encamping at Luokou.
proposals.reason: 聖善寺 is Shengshan (Sacred Goodness) Temple; Shenshan is a mistranscription of the temple name.

proposals.before: The subordinate general Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi contested possession of Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Jing at Shenshan Temple; seizing victory, he wished to attack Heyang and encamped at Luokou.
proposals.after: The subordinate general Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi contested possession of Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Jing at Shengshan Temple; seizing victory, he wished to attack Heyang and encamped at Luokou.
proposals.reason: 聖善寺 should be romanized Shengshan, not Shenshan, matching the Chinese characters.

proposals.before: (《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》: Whenever the Prince was pleased with a household's farming and weaving, if some family that year had good silkworms and wheat within one li of the capital, he would certainly ride there on horseback, summon all the old and young of that family, personally comfort and encourage them, and bestow wine, food, tea, and colored goods; to the men he gave cloth trousers, to the women skirts and jackets; at the time the common people still favored blue clothing, and the women all had theirs made of blue silk.
proposals.after: (《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》: Whenever the Prince was pleased with a household's farming and weaving, if some family that year had good silkworms and wheat within one she (a day's journey) of the capital, he would certainly ride there on horseback, summon all the old and young of that family, personally comfort and encourage them, and bestow wine, food, tea, and colored goods; to the men he gave cloth trousers, to the women skirts and jackets; at the time the common people still favored blue clothing, and the women all had theirs made of blue silk.
proposals.reason: 一舍 is a day's travel distance, not one li; the literal wrongly renders 舍 as li.

proposals.before: The Founder of Liang forced Emperor Zhaozong to move east and ordered Quanyi to repair the Luoyang palace city; only after many years was it gathered together.
proposals.after: The Founder of Liang forced Emperor Zhaozong to move east and ordered Quanyi to repair the Luoyang palace city; only after many years was it completed.
proposals.reason: 累年方集 here means the multi-year repair was finally finished, not that the palace city was 'gathered together'.

proposals.before: (《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》 notes that the Prince of Qi and the Liang Founder had both served as central secretariat ministers; when the Founder took four commands concurrently, the Prince repeatedly asked to yield his concurrent posts, having sensed the Founder's ambition and seeking to keep himself safe.
proposals.after: (《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》 notes that the Prince of Qi and the Liang Founder had each served as Minister of the Central Secretariat and Minister of the Imperial Secretariat; when the Founder took four commands concurrently, the Prince repeatedly asked to yield his concurrent posts, having sensed the Founder's ambition and seeking to keep himself safe.
proposals.reason: 互為中書令、尚書令 names two distinct offices; the idiomatic rendering collapses them into a single vague 'central secretariat ministers'.

proposals.before: When, after the Founder of Liang lost his army in Hebei and Shuo, each month he presented armor and horses to replenish his forces;
proposals.after: After the Founder of Liang lost his army in Hebei and Shuo, each month he presented armor and horses to replenish his forces;
proposals.reason: Opening 'When, after' is ungrammatical and obscures that Quanyi (silent subject) presents the armor and horses after the Founder's Hebei defeat.

proposals.before: Quanyi's wife was the Chu clan; she was bright, keen, and had stratagems.
proposals.after: Quanyi's wife was Lady Chu; she was bright, keen, and had stratagems.
proposals.reason: 儲氏 names Quanyi's wife of the Chu surname (Lady Chu), not that his wife 'was the Chu clan'.

proposals.before: (《Unofficial Biography of the Prince of Qi》 records that the Founder suspected the Prince and tried four times to kill him; Lady Chu pleaded with him in person and saved her husband; the Founder then had his son the Prince of Fu marry the Prince of Qi's daughter.)〉
proposals.after: (The Unofficial Biography of the Prince of Qi records that the Founder suspected the Prince and tried four times to kill him; Lady Chu pleaded with him in person and saved her husband; the Founder then had his son the Prince of Fu marry the Prince of Qi's daughter.)
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English fuses a Chinese book-title bracket into the English title and leaves a stray closing Chinese bracket, obscuring the citation.

proposals.before: The emperor comforted him at length, had attendants help the old man up the hall, feasted him generously, and ordered Prince Jiji, Prince Cunji, and others to treat him as an elder brother.
proposals.after: The emperor comforted him at length, had attendants help the old man up the hall, feasted him generously, and ordered the imperial son Jiji, the imperial brother Cunji, and others to treat him as an elder brother.
proposals.reason: Chinese distinguishes 皇子繼岌 and 皇弟存紀; idiomatic wrongly calls both Prince.

proposals.before: Quanyi stopped him, saying, "At Heyang I once endured Li Hanzhi's siege for a year, eating wood shavings day to day and expecting death at any moment until another saved me and brought me to today—that debt cannot be repaid with betrayal."
proposals.after: Quanyi stopped him, saying, "When I was lately at Heyang and met Li Hanzhi's calamity, he brought the Taiyuan army to besiege us for a full year; I ate wood shavings day to day and expected death at any moment until another rescued me and brought me to today—this grace cannot be betrayed."
proposals.reason: Idiomatic fuses 'Heyang I', omits Taiyuan army, and weakens 恩不可負 as debt rather than unrepayable grace.

proposals.before: He later entered the service of Wang Hong, military governor of Shanzhou, and rose by merit to regimental commander.
proposals.after: He later entered the service of Wang Gong, military governor of Shanzhou, and rose by merit to regimental commander.
proposals.reason: Chinese 王珙 is Wang Gong (珙 gǒng); Hong is an incorrect romanization of the given name.

proposals.before: Later he served the Shanzhou military governor Wang Hong and through accumulated merit reached army commander.
proposals.after: Later he served the Shanzhou military governor Wang Gong and through accumulated merit reached army commander.
proposals.reason: Chinese 王珙 must be Wang Gong; Hong misreads 珙.

proposals.before: Wang Hong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
proposals.after: Wang Gong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
proposals.reason: Continues wrong romanization Wang Hong for 珙/王珙.

proposals.before: Wang Hong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
proposals.after: Wang Gong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
proposals.reason: Literal line repeats Wang Hong for 珙; correct to Wang Gong.

proposals.before: In 898 Wang Hong and his brother Ke, military governor of Hezhong, fell into open war; Hong's armies kept losing and his troops lost heart.
proposals.after: In 898 Wang Gong and his brother Ke, military governor of Hezhong, fell into open war; Gong's armies kept losing and his troops lost heart.
proposals.reason: Wang Hong/Hong should be Wang Gong/Gong for 珙.

proposals.before: In the first year of Guanghua, Hong and his younger brother the Hezhong military governor Ke confronted each other; arms were sought day by day; Hong's troops repeatedly were defeated; the ranks lost heart.
proposals.after: In the first year of Guanghua, Gong and his younger brother the Hezhong military governor Ke confronted each other; arms were sought day by day; Gong's troops repeatedly were defeated; the ranks lost heart.
proposals.reason: Hong standing for 珙 should be Gong.

proposals.before: In the sixth month of the following year Fan killed Hong, went over to the Liang, and the Liang Founder had him appointed military governor of Shanzhou.
proposals.after: In the sixth month of the following year Fan killed Gong, went over to the Liang, and the Liang Founder had him appointed military governor of Shanzhou.
proposals.reason: Hong here is 珙 and should be Gong.

proposals.before: In the sixth month of the second year Fan killed Hong, submitted to the Bian men, and the Founder of Liang memorialized Fan as military governor of Shanzhou.
proposals.after: In the sixth month of the second year Fan killed Gong, submitted to the Bian men, and the Founder of Liang memorialized Fan as military governor of Shanzhou.
proposals.reason: Hong for 珙 is incorrect; use Gong.

proposals.before: The Luoyang army supervisor once obtained the sobering stone from Director Li's Pingquan estate; Quanyi sought it; the supervisor would not give it; Quanyi immediately killed him—his clinging to power and making might were again thus.
proposals.after: The Luoyang army supervisor once obtained the sobering stone from Grand Commandant Li's Pingquan estate; Quanyi sought it; the supervisor would not give it; Quanyi immediately killed him—his clinging to power and making might were again thus.
proposals.reason: 太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Director; the literal office title is mistranslated.

proposals.before: Youqian said: "The Prince of Jin personally rushed to my urgency, at midnight bore candles to fight the enemy, face to face made covenant oath, and will not betray the first heart.
proposals.after: Youqian said: "The Prince of Jin personally rushed to my urgency, at midnight bore candles to fight the enemy, and face to face made a covenant oath; I will not betray that original resolve.
proposals.reason: The clause 不負初心 is Youqian's own pledge, not a continuation of the Prince of Jin as grammatical subject.

proposals.before: Yesterday I heard of my reporting difficulty; he ordered the general to march by starlight, aided my provisions and grain, divided my clothes and shoes—yet you wish to turn over and betray grace; this is what is called Duke Qi of Deng's saying, 'Men will not eat what I leave over.'
proposals.after: When recently he heard of my crisis, he ordered generals to march by starlight, aided me with provisions and grain, and shared clothes and footwear with me—yet you wish to turn and betray that grace; this is what Duke Qi of Deng meant by saying, 'Men will not eat what I leave over.'
proposals.reason: 昨聞吾告難 takes the Prince of Jin as hearer; 分我衣屨 means sharing clothing with Youqian, not dividing Youqian's clothes.

proposals.before: Emperor Zhuangzong set a feast to feast and comfort him, favor and gifts without reckoning; he personally poured the goblet and entrusted Youqian, saying: "He who completed my great enterprise—you, sir, are the force."
proposals.after: Emperor Zhuangzong set a feast to feast and comfort him, with favor and gifts beyond reckoning; he personally poured the goblet and toasted Youqian, saying: "He who completed my great enterprise—you, sir, are the force."
proposals.reason: 屬 here is a toast urging the cup on Youqian, not 'entrust'.

proposals.before: His sons Lingde and Lingxi were made military governors of Suizhou and Xuzhou.
proposals.after: His sons Lingde and Lingxi were made military governors of Suizhou and Xu Prefecture.
proposals.reason: 許州 is Xu Prefecture (around Xuchang), not the identically romanized Xuzhou 徐州.

proposals.reason: Same title error as idiomatic: 篡誤 here denotes the correction treatise Zuanwu, not usurpation.
